site/src/data/forecast-examples/july-2026-wave.ts:208:        "text": "Prior/update/interval: persistence prior is the latest DOL print of 215 thousand blended with the recent six-week mean of 220.8 and four-week average of 222.0. site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:6072:          text: "The resolver is the first-print national seasonally adjusted initial claims figure in the ETA weekly claims report for the week ending June 20, 2026; the unit here is thousands of claims.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:6077:          call: "Opened DOL current weekly claims PDF at https://www.dol.gov/ui/data.pdf.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:6079:            "Fetched latest report embargoed until 8:30 A.M. Eastern Thursday, June 18, 2026; week ending June 13 seasonally adjusted initial claims were 226,000; previous week revised to 230,000; 4-week moving average was 223,250.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:6086:            "Fetched June 18, 2026 release summary: week ending June 13 initial claims 226,000, decrease 4,000 from revised 230,000; June 11 release summary: week ending June 6 initial claims 229,000 before later revision; June 4 summary: week ending May 30 initial claims 225,000.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:6091:          call: "Opened FRED ICSA page at https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/ICSA for history mirror and release-date check.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:6101:          text: "Recent anchors: 3-week average = (226 + 230 + 225) / 3 = 227.0; 5-week average = (226 + 230 + 225 + 212 + 210) / 5 = 220.6; latest 4-week average = 223.25. I put the point at 225, slightly below the 3-week average but above the 5-week average because early-June claims have been elevated versus May.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:6611:          text: "The 356 to 385 interval implies a May-to-October increment range of 31.243 to 60.243 billion around the 324.757 billion May anchor. The lower tail allows front-loading or processing delays to pull the remaining increment below the recent 36.672 to 42.137 billion band, while the upper tail allows policy-driven late-filer refund claims to add much more than the short three-year reference class.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:18134:        "Initial claims remain low but the four-week average has risen",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:18266:          call: "Checked the latest official DOL unemployment insurance weekly claims release for layoff pressure near the survey month.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:18268:            "DOL reported initial claims of 226,000 for the week ending Jun. 13, 2026, down 4,000 from the revised 230,000 prior week; the 4-week moving average was 223,250, up 4,000; insured unemployment was 1,810,000 for the week ending Jun. 6.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:18272:          text: "Base rate: the last three available payroll changes average about 188 thousand using 214, 179, and 172. That is a strong starting point, but it likely overstates June because the latest claims average has moved up and May had unusually large leisure, hospitality, and local-government gains.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:18276:          text: "Counter-consideration: claims are still low by historical standards and BLS revised March and April up sharply, so a sudden weak or negative print is not the central case. The main risk is normal first-print noise, not a clear labor-market break.",
site/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:18280:          text: "I start from the recent 188 thousand three-month average, shade down roughly 45 thousand for mild claims deterioration and possible payback from May strength, then round to 140 thousand. An 80% first-print interval of 35 to 245 thousand allows about +/-105 thousand around the point, consistent with volatile monthly CES surprises.",

This is not the official poverty measure: SPM resources add taxes, refundable credits, and noncash transfers, and subtract necessary expenses including medical and work expenses, with thresholds adjusted for housing tenure and geography.\\\\\\\",\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10462:            \\\\\\\"Fetched annual first-print publication dates of 2025-09-09 for calendar-year 2024 data and 2024-09-10 for calendar-year 2023 data; no official 2028 calendar entry for calendar-year 2027 poverty data was available in the checked Census calendar at run time.\\\\\\\",\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10474:          text: \\\\\\\"Policy mechanism: the child SPM rate is unusually exposed to refundable tax credits, SNAP, school meals, housing subsidies, medical expenses, and child-care/work-expense deductions. For 2027, my central case assumes no broad permanent 2021-style child allowance is in force for the full year, so taxes and transfers keep the rate near the post-pandemic plateau rather than returning to 2021's 5.2 percent.\\\\\\\",\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10478:          text: \\\\\\\"Counter-consideration: a material labor-market weakening by 2027 or benefit cuts could push the rate above 17 percent, while a large refundable child-credit expansion, unusually strong real wage growth for low-income families, or lower out-of-pocket medical and child-care costs could move it below 12 percent.\\\\\\\",\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:10482:          text: \\\\\\\"Point calculation: start from a weighted recent baseline of 13.7 percent using 2022-2024 values, add +0.3 for loss of residual pandemic-era supports and higher SPM expense pressure by 2027, add +0.2 for recession/policy asymmetry because downside poverty risks are larger than upside income surprises, giving 14.2 percent. Interval: using the non-2021-reversal post-expiration evidence, 2022 to 2023 was +1.3 pp and 2023 to 2024 was +0.1 pp, while 2019 to 2024 was +1.2 pp; I treat roughly +/-2.5 pp as normal 80 percent uncertainty around 14.2, then widen and right-skew judgmentally for tax-credit, benefit, and labor-market tail risk to 11.5 to 17.4.\\\\\\\",\\\\nrecords/2026-06-22/digest.json:86: I use 13.4 percent as the current-policy outside-view anchor before adding the conditional $3,000 fully refundable CTC.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2635:          text: \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Time-series prior: I do not extrapolate a simple linear trend because the child SPM series has large policy discontinuities from pandemic stimulus, expanded refundable credits, and their expiration; a persistence prior around the recent non-expanded-CTC level is more defensible.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2639:          text: \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Policy mechanism: a fully refundable $3,000 CTC would count in SPM tax-credit resources for eligible families and would matter most for children in low-earnings households who receive little or no current-law nonrefundable credit. It should not mechanically recreate the 2021 5.2 percent rate because the 2021 outcome also reflected larger under-age-6 credits, stimulus payments, and pandemic-era safety-net conditions.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2643:          text: \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Anchor 13.4 percent. Subtract 4.7 percentage points for the $3,000 fully refundable CTC, smaller than the 7.2 point 2021-to-2022 child SPM reversal because this condition excludes stimulus and the $3,600 young-child amount. Point = 13.4 - 4.7 = 8.7. For the 80% interval, combine about 1.3 points of recent annual child-SPM movement, roughly 1.5-2.0 points of policy-effect uncertainty, and macro/SPM modeling risk, giving an asymmetric judgmental interval of 5.7 to 12.0.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:2647:          text: \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Counter-consideration: an outcome near 5.7 percent or lower could happen if wage growth is broad, housing and food burdens ease, and refundable-credit take-up is near-complete. I use 2022 and 2023 child SPM values plus the 2024 overall SPM signal. After the 2021 refundable-credit expansion expired, child SPM returned to low-to-mid teens, with 2021 at 5.2% treated as an exceptional policy year.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3164:          text: \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Policy mechanism: under the condition, a House-style TCJA extension prevents the child credit from falling back toward the pre-TCJA $1,000 structure, which is poverty-reducing versus expiration. But the extension is not the 2021 fully refundable CTC and therefore does much less for the lowest-income children than the ARPA design that produced the 5.2% child SPM rate.\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\",\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\nsite/src/data/thesis-analyst-live-comparisons.ts:3168:          text: \\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\\"Counter-consideration: if the enacted package preserves more SNAP, Medicaid-linked expense protection, or refundable child credit value than assumed, child SPM could fall toward 11%.
